newsitem.title: USA: Overweight core LatAm debt in '97 - Merrill's Chang.
newsitem.headline: Overweight core LatAm debt in '97 - Merrill's Chang.

text.p: Emerging markets debt portfolios should be well-stocked with core Latin American credits in 1997, said Merrill Lynch chief emerging markets debt strategist Joyce Chang.
"We would recommend ... overweight positions in core credits such as Brazil, Mexico and Venezuela," Chang told reporters at a press conference here on Tuesday.
Those three countries "have lower refinancing needs than some of the other Latin American countries and are much better cushioned against market volatility," she said.
Chang recommended underweighting Panama and Peru.
Chang forecast emerging markets debt would, in dollars, return perhaps 15 percent in 1997, compared with about 31.5 percent so far in 1996.

"We do not believe the performance we saw in 1995 and 1996 is likely to be repeated next year, although we do believe the market sentiment will remain positive and the global conditions are positive," Chang said.

Spread compression will not match its 1996 levels next year, Chang predicted. Brady bond spreads shrank an average of 470 basis points this year, but should decline about 100 to 150 basis points in 1997, she said.

Fundamentals appear strong in many emerging economies, she said. Gross Domestic Product should expand 4.3 percent in the Latin American region next year, up from 3.3 percent in 1996, according to Chang.

Growth should perk up in Central and Eastern Europe as well, despite some recent shabby performances, Chang said. She recommended overweighting Croatia and Russia and underweighting Bulgaria and Turkey.
Record issuance of some $67 billion in 1996 might suggest unsustainable debt burdens, but Chang said that is not the case.
"That still gets you returns that are around 15 percent, in some cases even higher," Chang said.
New money is key to market performance next year, with emerging markets seeming expensive to dedicated fund managers but attractive to new investors, Chang said.
"We're quite optimistic this new crossover investor is going to find the market compelling" when compared to U.S. high-yield debt, Chang said.
"We believe we are in a virtuous cycle," Chang said, pointing out the longer maturities and narrower yields many emerging countries have achieved.
